assessment_summary: The statement asserts that a stable matching is unique when preferences are strict and complete. This is famously false. I have provided a concrete 2-man, 2-woman instance where the man-optimal stable matching and the woman-optimal stable matching are distinct, thus showing the stable matching is not unique.
counterexample:
Consider n=2 with men {m1, m2} and women {w1, w2}.
Preferences:
m1: w1 > w2
m2: w2 > w1
w1: m2 > m1
w2: m1 > m2

Matching 1: {(m1, w1), (m2, w2)}. This is stable because both men are assigned their first-choice partners; therefore, no man will ever prefer another woman to his current partner, meaning no blocking pair can exist.
Matching 2: {(m1, w2), (m2, w1)}. This is stable because both women are assigned their first-choice partners; similarly, no woman will ever prefer another man to her current partner, meaning no blocking pair can exist.

Since both Matching 1 and Matching 2 are valid stable matchings for this instance, the stable matching is not unique.
